newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS - S.Africa's Manuel cautious on forex controls.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - S.Africa's Manuel cautious on forex controls.

text.p: South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel on Tuesday reaffirmed his commitment to abolishing exchange controls, but said he had no final deadline and was not talking to the IMF about a standby facility.

In a news briefing wrapping up the 1996 session of South Africa's first democratic parliament, Manuel said he expected soon to reap the benefit of the government's commitment to fiscal discipline and his own macro-economic strategy.

Manuel said the strategy, promising accelerated economic growth premised on fiscal discipline and improved non-gold exports, was likely soon to reverse the decline in the value of the South African rand.
The rand has lost 28 percent of its value since mid-February, when false rumours about President Nelson Mandela's health triggered a slide.
"We are likely to see more durable kinds of results. We do expect certain rewards," Manuel said.

In an apparent repudiation of rising pressure from the private sector, however, Manuel said it was not time to lift remaining foreign exchange controls or to take up an offered International Monetary Fund (IMF) standby facility.
He said he had no final deadline for the abolition of exchange controls and, for the first time, raised the prospect of continued controls in the form of a prudential requirement on savings.
South African Chamber of Business (Sacob) director of economic policy told a news conference in Johannesburg there were fears that the decline in the rand could destabilise the whole economy.

"The government must bring the IMF into the picture. When we experience a balance of payments problem, we must be able to make use of the IMF's standby facility.... We need to let speculators know we are not on our own," he said.
IMF managing director Michel Camdessus visited South Africa last month, offering a $2 billion facility on the basis of Manuel's macro-economic blueprint without further conditions.
The Finance Minister said on Tuesday that an IMF facility remained an option for South Africa, but added that the fund should be seen as a lender of last resort.
"We remain in discussion with the (central) Reserve Bank. The finger is on the pulse. But I'm not suggesting we are in discussion with the IMF about the standby facility," he said.

Manuel said foreign reserves, which, at 10 billion rand, were equivalent to only four weeks of imports at the end of September, were too low to allow for an immediate abolition of exchange controls, which apply only to residents.
"It's not about policy. It is tied into your reserve position at any given time. If you have a high level of reserves, I think you have more manoeuverability," he said.
Camdessus told reporters during his visit that the IMF facility - which would more than double foreign reserves - could be used to bolster the capital account during a phase of liberalisation.
But members of the ruling African National Congress criticised Camdessus and the fund during a public meeting, calling the IMF a "witchdoctor".
Manuel was more sympathetic on Tuesday, saying South Africa had to acknowledge the existence of the IMF and the World Bank and their expertise.
